passage.title: Sixteen Grams of Balsa Wood
passage.author: BEACON Assessment Lab
passage.text:
On the morning of the regional Science Olympiad, Mateo held their balsa-wood bridge in both palms as if it were spun glass. The entire frame weighed just sixteen grams, less than a handful of coins. Across the gym floor, his partner Priya was already adjusting her safety goggles with a wide grin. Where Mateo saw fragile matchsticks ready to snap, Priya saw a web of triangles built to fight gravity. They had glued fifty-two thin strips together over three weeks of after-school practice.

When the judge called their school name, they set the bridge across the twenty-inch gap between two oak blocks. An iron loading block was threaded through the center of the bridge, and an empty five-gallon plastic bucket hung by a chain beneath it. The light wooden truss, glued in neat triangles by Priya and Mateo, was slowly pulled downward by the swinging metal hook. Mateo held his breath as the wood gave a tiny creak. Priya simply picked up the first brass scoop of dry river sand.

Scoop by scoop, Priya poured golden sand down the funnel tube into the hanging bucket. At five kilograms, the top beam bowed slightly, yet the side triangles locked tight to distribute the load toward the oak blocks. Mateo winced at every sharp pop of dried glue and took half a step back from the table. Priya leaned closer instead. She watched the symmetry of the side struts to make sure neither wall twisted out of line.

By the time the digital scale read twelve kilograms, a quiet crowd had gathered around the test stand. The thin balsa strips trembled under the immense strain, and a hairline crack appeared near the left pin. Mateo squeezed his eyes shut as Priya poured one last steady stream of sand into the chute. At fourteen point four kilograms, the bridge finally burst with a sound like a snapped dry twig, dropping the heavy bucket into the catch box.

Mateo opened his eyes and stared at the splintered sticks, sure they had failed because the bridge broke. Then he saw Priya pumping her fist while the judge circled their score at the top of the leaderboard. In Bridge Building, the goal was never to keep a bridge unbroken forever; it was to push sixteen grams of brittle wood to its highest possible limit.

tier2Words.definition: To spread out evenly across several parts or places

tier2Words.rootHint: stringere (Latin root meaning 'to draw tight' or 'press')

tier2Words.contextClue: The dry balsa wood 'burst with a sound like a snapped dry twig' into 'splintered sticks.'

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"The light wooden truss, glued in neat triangles by Priya and Mateo, was slowly pulled downward by the swinging metal hook."

In the main clause of this sentence, what pulled the light wooden truss downward?

options.text: Priya and Mateo, the two Science Olympiad partners
options.diagnosticNote: Confuses the agent inside the middle participial phrase ('glued... by Priya and Mateo') with the agent of the main verb ('was slowly pulled downward').
options.childFeedback: Careful—this choice confuses the noun inside the middle describing phrase ('glued... by Priya and Mateo') with who or what actually did the main action ('was slowly pulled downward').

options.text: The neat triangles of dried glue along the sides
options.diagnosticNote: Selects a noun phrase inside the descriptive modifier rather than the force pulling the truss down.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—this choice selects a noun phrase inside the middle describing phrase rather than the force pulling the truss down.

options.text: The swinging metal hook attached to the loading block
options.diagnosticNote: Correctly identifies the passive agent following the main verb ('was slowly pulled downward by the swinging metal hook').
options.childFeedback: Spot on! This answer correctly identifies the doer of the action following the main verb ('was slowly pulled downward by the swinging metal hook').

options.text: The light wooden truss resting on the oak blocks
options.diagnosticNote: Confuses the grammatical subject/receiver of the action ('The light wooden truss') with the actor performing the pulling.
options.childFeedback: Careful—this choice confuses the subject receiving the action of the action ('The light wooden truss') with the actor performing the pulling.

questions.provingSentenceText: The light wooden truss, glued in neat triangles by Priya and Mateo, was slowly pulled downward by the swinging metal hook.
questions.childTip: Spot on! This answer correctly identifies the doer of the action following the main verb ('was slowly pulled downward by the swinging metal hook').
questions.parentExplanation: Sentence Surgery (ELAGSE5L1). This sentence contains two 'by' phrases: 'by Priya and Mateo' modifies 'glued', whereas 'by the swinging metal hook' is the actor of the main passive verb 'was slowly pulled downward.'
questions.retryHint: In Paragraph 2, watch out for two 'by' phrases! Look right after 'was slowly pulled downward by' to find the real puller.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 3:

"At five kilograms, the top beam bowed slightly, yet the side triangles locked tight to distribute the load toward the oak blocks."

What does the word distribute mean as it is used in the sentence?

options.text: Spread the weight out across the structure
options.diagnosticNote: Matches the engineering context where the side triangles share and spread the downward weight out toward both oak support blocks.
options.childFeedback: Spot on! This answer matches the engineering context where the side triangles share and spread the downward weight out toward both oak support blocks.

options.text: Drop the entire bucket straight onto the gym floor
options.diagnosticNote: Contradicts the sentence, where the triangles lock tight to hold the five-kilogram load without breaking.
options.childFeedback: Not quite—this choice contradicts the sentence, where the triangles lock tight to hold the five-kilogram load without breaking.

options.text: Weigh the balsa wood on a digital scale
options.diagnosticNote: Confuses the action of the side triangles during the sand test with weighing the bridge.
options.childFeedback: Careful—this choice confuses the action of the side triangles during the sand test with weighing the bridge.

options.text: Glue extra strips of wood onto the top beam
options.diagnosticNote: Refers to building the bridge before the contest rather than how the triangles behave during the test.
options.childFeedback: Not quite—this choice refers to building the bridge before the contest rather than how the triangles behave during the test.

questions.provingSentenceText: At five kilograms, the top beam bowed slightly, yet the side triangles locked tight to distribute the load toward the oak blocks.
questions.childTip: Spot on! This answer matches the engineering context where the side triangles share and spread the downward weight out toward both oak support blocks.
questions.parentExplanation: Contextual Vocabulary (ELAGSE5RL4). Instead of letting the center beam snap under five kilograms, the side triangles 'locked tight to distribute the load toward the oak blocks,' meaning to spread the weight out.
questions.retryHint: In Paragraph 3, think about what triangles in a bridge do with heavy weight so one single spot doesn't snap right away.

questions.prompt: How does the third-person narrator's focus on Mateo's thoughts and feelings shape the reader's experience of the bridge test?

options.text: It explains the exact mathematical formulas the judge used to calculate scores for every other school in the gym.

options.text: It builds suspense during the test and makes the ending a surprise when the broken bridge wins first place.
options.diagnosticNote: Explains how following Mateo's worry (seeing 'spun glass', wincing at creaks, fearing failure when it snaps) creates tension and a rewarding final realization.
options.childFeedback: Spot on! This answer explains how following Mateo's worry (seeing 'spun glass', wincing at creaks, fearing failure when it snaps) creates tension and a rewarding final realization.

options.text: It shows that Mateo dislikes science contests and will never build a balsa-wood bridge again.

options.childFeedback: Watch out—this choice uses extreme language ('never... again') that misreads Mateo's protective care for his bridge as dislike.

questions.provingSentenceText: Mateo opened his eyes and stared at the splintered sticks, sure they had failed because the bridge broke.

questions.parentExplanation: Focus standard ELAGSE5RL6 (Point of View & Perspective). By filtering the test largely through Mateo's protective anxiety, the narrator keeps the reader on edge with every creak until Priya's celebration reveals the true goal of the event.

questions.prompt: PART A: Which statement best expresses a central theme of the story?

options.text: True strength is measured not by staying untouched, but by how much challenge something can endure before reaching its limit.
options.diagnosticNote: Captures the thematic realization in Paragraph 5 that success came from testing the sixteen-gram bridge to its highest possible limit.
options.childFeedback: Spot on! This answer captures the big lesson in Paragraph 5 that success came from testing the sixteen-gram bridge to its highest possible limit.

options.text: Heavy oak blocks are always stronger than balsa wood when building full-size highway bridges.
options.diagnosticNote: Focuses literally on the test stand blocks rather than the thematic lesson of the story.
options.childFeedback: Not quite—this choice focuses literally on the test stand blocks rather than the big lesson of the story.

options.text: Students who close their eyes during a science test will always win first place on the leaderboard.
options.diagnosticNote: Turns a minor detail of Mateo's nervousness into a false, extreme rule.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—this choice turns a minor detail of Mateo's nervousness into a false, extreme rule.

options.text: Partners who have different attitudes cannot work together successfully on an engineering project.
options.diagnosticNote: Contradicts the story, where Mateo's careful craftsmanship and Priya's bold testing win first place together.
options.childFeedback: Not quite—this choice contradicts the story, where Mateo's careful craftsmanship and Priya's bold testing win first place together.

questions.provingSentenceText: In Bridge Building, the goal was never to keep a bridge unbroken forever; it was to push sixteen grams of brittle wood to its highest possible limit.

questions.parentExplanation: Part A of the EBSR pair targets Theme (ELAGSE5RL2). Mateo learns that keeping the fragile bridge safe on a shelf is not the point; real achievement means testing what they built to its maximum capacity.
